This one missed me pretty hard, so I will just jump right into why. The quest for the maid's abortion B plot, seemed entirely unnecessary but alas, why waste all of our attention without making it absolutely clear the already blaringly obvious political message here. Also lets make sure the viewer knows it was a relatively late abortion too. Also a purely elective abortion. Glad we can always count on there being a local abortion clinic in the late 1700s. Lets have the characters later reenact the abortion again too and paint it as well. Just for the record, this is not a testament of where I side on the issue, but rather I dislike the ham-fisted delivery of the message. Which brings me to the A plot of the romance. The romance here feels painfully hollow,  and almost as if the film is aware of it, they try to overcompensate. Such as making every lesbian kissing scene leave long saliva strings after they separate. In all the kissing scenes I have watched throughout the years, I have never seen this, which leads me to believe this was an intended effect. Did they do takes without this and their romance was just not believable, so they had to up the ante with long saliva strings? The character development here is quite thin,  in almost a hubris, I feel like they are trying to develop characters through looks alone, but in my opinion I do not feel that the director or actors have the talent to pull this off. It was not all bad though, the film setting was top tier, the story was well thought out and well organized, and the cinematography was decent so it gets some points for that.

Nós temos aqui um tema que toca em assuntos como sexualidade feminina, lesbianismo e aborto no século XVIII, mas nada é aprofundado e contextualizado conforme a época em que se passa o filme, dando a impressão que tudo é contemporâneo senão fosse pela fotografia da casa onde as personagens vivem e seus figurinos. Você tem também a criada da casa que está grávida, não quer ter o filho e resolve abortar, nisto elas procuram quem faça e surgem do nada numa festa onde só há mulheres que não sabemos de onde surgiram e ao amanhecer somem. I have nothing intelligent to say about this film, not even anything I can disguise as intelligence. All I have is what I thought while watching, which consisted mostly of the thinking equivalent of an eye roll, or a scoff, maybe. When I am watching a film, the defining factor for me—which is a defining factor which builds the basis of “good art,” for me—is whether or not it invokes emotions, & if it does, what kinds of emotions? The amount of symbolism a film saturates itself w/, (this film includes color theory, metaphors, eroticism, babies, & whatnots) does not make it inherently better. Maybe it becomes more interesting in its conversations concerning itself, but it does not, in my opinion, make the film “better.” Rather, I think, a good film is good when it can (a) express emotions about humanity, & (b) do it in an interesting way(do not confuse interesting w/ lots of symbolism). This film does, in my opinion, does not stir emotion, & I didn’t find it particularly interesting in its expressions. For me, if a film has bad dialogue, it really turns me off of it, in terms of my interest in it, which I hope doesn’t make me sound pretentious, but this film didn’t have good dialogue, or rather, it didn’t have dialogue that I enjoyed. Most of the film just felt like one character asking another character a question, & the other says “Oui,” or “No,” & then they make eyes at each other for a solid thirty seconds. Those are the parts that, to me, felt the most hokey. Also, I thought that the characters were very melodramatic, which you could argue is because they’re two gay women experiencing love for the first time, but I feel like that’s just an excuse for bad writing. It’s possible to portray lesbian romances w/o making the characters act totally melodramatic(Desert Hearts & The Handmaiden are two that come to mind w/ my extremely lmtd knowledge). There were some parts I liked. I liked the part where she reads the myth of Orpheus. I thought the abortion scene was very well done(I thought Sophie was a very well done character in general). I like that there were no men in the film, because, like, to put men on the island would totally desacralize it. I like the final scene, with the music performance. &c. Not to mention that—& I know this might be totally solipsistic of me to say—the subjects that the film focus on aren’t exactly in my ball park of experiences, which usually isn’t the case for me. The first thing that caught me was how visually appealing it is. Cinematically, I can absolutely see why people praise this movie so much. The cinematography, the framing, the performances, and the overall presentation are beautiful. The story is about two women and the relationship that develops between them. I understood what the movie was trying to say, and I could see the depth of their connection. I've also seen people call this one of the most perfect romances ever made, and some even compared its emotional impact to Titanic. But honestly, it didn't hit me that way. For me, I was watching it as a movie rather than emotionally placing myself inside the relationship. Even during the final moments, when people say the movie becomes extremely emotional, I was honestly just thinking, "How long is this going to take?" That doesn't mean I think the movie is bad. Quite the opposite. I think it's an excellent film from a cinematic perspective, and I'm glad I explored something completely different. I believe this is also my first French movie. But emotionally, it just wasn't for me. ‘Portrait of a Lady on Fire’ is one of the most beautiful films I’ve ever seen. every single shot looks like a 19th century painting come alive. I kept wanting to pause it just to take in the composition because everything is so carefully framed and the lighting and colour grading is so gorgeous. this really does feel like a love letter to art, but also to the process of creating art and the women who have historically been reduced to being the subject rather than being recognised as artists themselves. the colour palette feels so intentional and I was thrilled with colour forming such a crucial part of the storytelling, which feels fitting for a movie focused around art. so much of the film is made up of warm, earthy tones - browns, creams, reds and greys. this makes the emerald green of Héloïse’s dress stand out so dramatically. she’s being dressed to be presented to a man she’s never met, turned into a portrait of which the sole purpose is to convince a complete stranger to marry her. the dress is impossible to ignore whenever it’s in frame as it feels so out of place. Héloïse looks beautiful in the dress, but somehow it doesn’t suit her - much like the marriage she’s expected to enter into. I love how much clothing tells us about these women throughout the film. Héloïse’s blue dress feels much more restrained and melancholic, whereas the green feels like a real shift in her character - she becomes more open to Marianne and to the possibility of choosing something for herself when she wears it, which is empowering. Marianne’s red dresses feel completely different - warmer, bolder, more passionate. there’s so much being communicated through colour without the film ever needing to explain it to us using dialogue. the entirety of ‘Portrait of a Lady on Fire’ feels like you’re watching a series of paintings come to life. the cliffs, the sea, the house, the beach, the women sitting around the fire… everything looks deliberately composed, even the simplest moments feel beautiful. I particularly loved how often the film focuses on people looking at each other. there’s so much meaning in a glance, especially because Marianne’s role is to look at Héloïse closely enough to secretly paint her. the more Marianne looks at her, the more Héloïse becomes a person to her rather than simply the subject of a commission. then, eventually, Héloïse starts looking back and the women open up to each other emotionally, then romantically. fire also feels like a character in this film. it’s everywhere! fireplaces, candles, the bonfire, the flames surrounding the women, and the moment when Héloïse’s dress catches fire. it’s such an interesting recurring image because fire can be warm and comforting, but it can also destroy things completely. fire burns quickly, the flames dancing spectacularly, the devastation is mesmerising - but then all that’s left is ash. fire feels like desire, anger, freedom and danger all at once. the bonfire scene in particular is incredible. Héloïse’s dress is accidentally set on fire while looking at Marianne, its significance being that their attraction is becoming impossible to ignore. everything in this film is so intentional that I want to watch this again purely to keep track of every time fire appears because I’m convinced there could be a hidden meaning behind how and when it’s used. there’s something so heartbreaking about the idea that Marianne and Héloïse’s relationship is relatively short, but the love they felt for each other was so passionate and sincere that it stayed with them for the rest of their lives. they can’t have each other, but their feelings are evergreen. I had a lump in my throat when Marianne saw a recent painting of Héloïse, and noticed that in the portrait, the book she was holding was partially open to reveal page 28 - the page on which Marianne had painted her own likeness for Héloïse to keep as a momento of their time together. this detail says so much about how Héloïse has carried Marianne in her heart all these years. the following scene broke me even more. Marianne notices Héloïse at a Vivaldi concert, with ‘Summer’ from ‘The Four Seasons’ playing - the same piece Marianne played for her on the piano earlier in the film. Héloïse doesn’t see Marianne, but she sits alone, away from her family, completely absorbed in the music. she looks completely transported back to that summer with Marianne, and you can see that she still misses her and still loves her. watching Héloïse experience all of those memories again, completely unaware that Marianne is sitting there watching her, was devastating. the ending was so emotionally charged that even I, a woman who has struggled to cry for the past few months, shed a few pathetic tears.

Portrait de la Jeune Fille en Feu Na solidão, senti a liberdade de que você falou. Mas também senti sua ausência Se o melodrama surge perante o sentimentalismo, sobretudo, a partir do exagero emocional, Celine Sciamma nos entrega o mais puro suco daquilo que o gênero significa. A primeira aparição de Héloïse é completamente carregada pela incógnita perante a quem é esta mulher, encapuzada, apenas abre a porta e se lança ao mundo, poucos passos são necessários para que seu capuz caia e se repouse em suas costas, assim revelando seus cabelos loiros, amarrados em um pequeno e bagunçado coque, todo o ar de imponência que era usado ao se referir a ela cai a partir do momento em que se percebe que ela mesmo que arrumou seu cabelo. Entretanto, a curiosidade por sua aparência não apenas se mantém como intensifica, quem é Héloïse? Poucos segundos se passam até o momento em que finalmente Marianne tem seus olhares voltados aos da jovem, contudo, mesmo após, nenhuma resposta é respondida, os olhos que anteriormente pareciam ser a resposta se mostram ainda mais enigmáticos. Se me for permitido, quero poder adicionar mais uma característica altamente intrínseca ao melodrama: a identificação da finitude do amor, ambas sabiam plenamente que cada traço de tinta que Marianne deixava ao quadro a distanciava mais de Héloïse, que ao pintar o amor de sua vida, estava fadando o fim do mesmo, entretanto, inevitável fim. Portrait de la Jeune Fille en Feu surge como um grande marco não apenas ao gênero, mas a todo o cinema Se Bergman inventou o cinema 2 em Persona, Sciamma aqui inventou o cinema 3

Such an extraordinarily tender film, so slow and gentle, yet without a single second feeling wasted. One particularly striking aspect of this film is the use of silence and ambient sound. Early on this silence feels repressive, almost choking at times. Sound and music is used sparingly, but when it is present it is extremely cathartic. Waves violently breaking on the cliffs allow stolen glances, piano music welcomes brief closeness and intimacy, the thumping of cards brings shared laughter, the drone and sweet hum of the singing crowd a mutual look of tender understanding. Even in their first kiss the silence is too overpowering. However Marianne and Héloïse gradually break down that silence together until it bursts asunder, although not through violent noise, but instead a new silence, not repressive but intimate. Yet still they know that what they have must be fleeting and at times that very silence becomes suppressive, even oppressive, again. Together by the roaring waves they can be real, genuine, together. But not in the quiet false society. In a quiet moment Marianne has her look back, her last shared moment and goodbye. The storm has finally broken. The music at the end allows Héloïse a brief respite from the false life like she was told earlier it would, for her to feel and love and remember, her moments to escape from a society where they cannot be together. I am also a sucker for anything Orpheus and Eurydice related, and I believe this film to be one of the most interesting interpretations of the myth. Beautifully heartbreaking and heartbreakingly beautiful.

What I love most is how the film tackles patriarchy without ever turning its ideas into speeches. It builds its argument through the way Marianne and Héloïse look at each other, paint each other, and gradually learn to exist as equals. Marianne first observes Héloïse in secret, treating her almost like an object to be studied and reproduced. "If you look at me, who do I look at?" Héloïse reveals that she has been learning Marianne’s gestures just as closely as Marianne has studied hers. The woman being painted has her own gaze, her own interpretation. Being seen becomes mutual, and equality begins when the observer accepts that she, too, is being observed. Consent changes the portrait in the same way. The first painting fails because it is made through secrecy and convention. Once she agrees to pose, the portrait becomes collaborative. Their love may ultimately be constrained by a patriarchal society that has already decided what Héloïse's future should look like, but the relationship itself refuses those same rules. It is built on reciprocity, consent, and recognition rather than possession. And when physical togetherness becomes impossible, art and memory preserve what society could not accommodate, not as a substitute for the life they might have shared, but as proof that it existed and permanently changed them. Patriarchy can dictate the shape of Héloïse's public life, but it cannot completely control how she loved, what she remembers, or the part of herself that survives in Marianne's art.

Portrait of a Lady on Fire (2019) Directed by Céline Sciamma Rating: 10 / 10 | Masterpiece ​Portrait of a Lady on Fire brought me to tears. It is a masterpiece that transcends usual romantic boundaries and clichés, burning down the traditional rules of the genre to create a love story that feels entirely, breathtakingly new. It starts on an isolated island, where a talented artist named Marianne (Noémie Merlant) is commissioned for a nearly impossible task: to paint the wedding portrait of Héloïse (Adèle Haenel), a young woman fiercely resisting her impending arranged marriage. Because Héloïse refuses to pose, Marianne must act as a walking companion by day, clandestinely stealing forbidden glances to memorize her subject's features to paint by night. What begins as a tense game of observation slowly ignites into a smoldering slow-burn of impossible yearning. As their walls crumble, the act of looking transforms into an explosive, deeply reciprocal romance with a devastatingly clear end. Director Céline Sciamma delivers something miraculous by entirely eliminating the male gaze. She actively strips away traditional power dynamics, ensuring the leads are on exact equal footing. The chemistry between Noémie Merlant and Adèle Haenel is electric; their bond, much like the portrait itself, is profoundly collaborative. But Sciamma’s boldest, most brilliant choice is the absence of a manipulative score. She packs every single frame with tangible emotion relying purely on Claire Mathon's luscious, warm cinematography and the visceral, ambient sounds of crashing waves and breathing. It is not just your love story. It explains the crushing tragedy of memory and the inevitability of loss. It brilliantly weaves in the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, challenging us to understand the difference between making the "lover's choice" and the "poet's choice." Haunted by the ghost of their sizzling final farewell, the film teaches us a brutal truth: the perfect song seldom plays during our most formative moments, and the perfect person seldom enters our lives at the right time. But choosing to remember them keeps the fire blazing long after the romance ends. It is really a gorgeous, devastatingly heartbreaking, and genuinely might be one of the best films I have ever seen. It is a story that is uniquely lesbian at its core, yet its profound meditation on the sting of lost love makes it starkly, beautifully universal.
